facts.statement: The disappearance was reported on a Tuesday morning, two days after the man was last seen at the river market.
A second, unsigned version of the last witness statement appears in the reopened case file.
The original statement notebook is still held by the clerk who took it that year.
Both crashes on the coastal road happened at night, in clear weather, on the same stretch of road.
Neither crash site showed brake marks on the road surface.
Phone records place both drivers on the same incoming call shortly before the two crashes.
The case was reopened twenty years after the disappearance, after an unsigned letter reached the local newspaper.
The newspaper kept no record of who delivered the letter, and the envelope carried no stamp and no postmark.
In the reopened file, the last witness's statement page is a replacement on different paper, typed in a different typeface.
The last witness's statement describes him leaving the river market alone, but records no hour for it.
The clerk who filed the original case retired years before the letter arrived and was never interviewed about the swap.
The missing man had lived in the riverside town for three years and was not known to have quarrels or debts.
The conviction later recognised as wrongful rested on a statement read out in court.
The first statement taken at the station differs from the court version in both wording and length.
The clerk's private notebook from that year matches the station version rather than the court version.
The accused withdrew his first statement before the trial, saying it did not read the way he had spoken.
The notebook runs without gaps and was never entered as evidence in the original proceedings.
The court record places the first statement's signing a day later than the date the clerk's notebook carries.
The wrongful-conviction finding came decades after the trial, in an administrative review.
The two crashes on the coastal stretch happened ten years apart.
Both drivers were alone in their cars; neither could be interviewed afterwards.
The two drivers did not know each other and lived in different provinces.
Both crash reports record the weather as dry with good visibility.
The incoming call each driver took before the crash came from the same phone number.
The stretch of road was resurfaced once between the two crashes; the second investigation file does not mention the resurfacing.
A new investigator reopened the comparison after noticing the shared phone number while digitising old files.
